reason: The attack I mounted was on the gap between the evidence and the source line: the verifier checked poets.org, which prints the Collected Poems text of 1994, while the source line names The Crisis, December 1922, so the card claims a printing the verifier never opened. I closed that gap rather than refuting on it. The Lehigh African American Poetry digital anthology transcribes the poem within its series LANGSTON HUGHES, POEMS PUBLISHED IN THE CRISIS 1921 to 1926 and states ‘First published in The Crisis, December 1922’; its opening lines are ‘Well, son, I’ll tell you:’ and ‘Life for me ain’t been no crystal stair.’, colon and full stop as the card has them, and the rest of that transcription carries the dialect spellings I’se and a-climbin’ that mark a period text rather than a modernised one. So the wording does exist in the printing the source names, and it happens to be identical in the modern text. The evidence field should cite that transcription alongside poets.org, which is a strengthening, not a correction. Attribution is not in doubt and nothing on the misattribution list touches it. Speaker: the poem is an unframed monologue in the mother’s voice and the title already names her, so the rule about naming a character in the source does not bite; adding ‘(the mother)’ after a locator on a poem called Mother to Son would be noise. Not shipped, no near match, Hughes at zero of three, not banned, no other May proposal uses him. In scope at 1922, publishable, verse lineation kept with the slash, curly apostrophes, source line 72 characters leading with the name. Tag Poetry is the form. The one objection I could not dismiss outright, and hand to the board: the card stops at line two, so it prints the adviser’s hardship and never reaches the advice, which arrives at lines 14 to 16, ‘So boy, don’t you turn back. / Don’t you set down on the steps / ’Cause you finds it’s kinder hard.’ For a month themed Wisdom and Counsel that is a real question. I did not refute on it because the colon in line one announces counsel and the card is headed by the poem’s own title, so the reader does receive the frame, and because the lines are the poem’s fame signal. If the board disagrees, the swap is to the same poem and the same 1922 printing and needs only a new locator.
